items.prompt: Does this prayer change how we should see the elders, who once drove the stranger out? Defend your view from the petition itself.
items.expected: Yes, the song marks a change, even if it does not rewrite the whole play in these few lines. The same chorus that once ordered the stranger away now asks that he be sped gently, spared pain, and blessed by Justice after a life they call wrongful oppression. That is a petition for peace, not a claim that they have always been kind. The ode leaves the stranger still on his way; it does not tell us what a later messenger will say, and it should be read as a religious song of escort and blessing, spoken as he goes.

items.prompt: How should we hold together the appeal to Justice and the appeal to the watch-dog in this ode?

satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”?
options: The Colonus ode
A plea that the powers below add further punishment
The elders’ prayer for his peace
The summons
satQuestions.explanation: The twenty-line ode is the elders’ prayer for their guest’s peace: they ask the powers below to “Speed this stranger to the gloom” by a “gentle, tearless doom” and to let “Justice” bless a man “Wrongfully in life oppressed” (Chorus, lines 1610–1615). It is not the earlier Colonus praise-ode, not a plea that the powers below add further punishment, and not the thunder-summons that has already called him away.

segments.activity: Say that the ode is short, read it aloud twice, and frame the prayer.
segments.script: Tell the class plainly: this is the shortest section of the play, a 20-line ode of about a hundred words, so today we read it closely and then write. Read all 20 lines aloud twice, in two voices (one for lines 1606–1615, one for lines 1616–1625). Then frame it: Oedipus has just left the stage, leading Theseus and his daughters toward the place where he must end, and the elders who stayed behind can follow him only in prayer. They call on the powers below, the unseen goddess, Aidoneus (another name for Hades) and the watch-dog at the gates, and ask one thing for their guest: that his going be gentle.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “By a gentle, tearless doom / Speed this stranger to the gloom, / Let him enter without pain / The all-shrouding Stygian plain” slowly and put it in my own words: The elders ask the god of the dead to send this stranger down gently, without tears and without pain. Next, craft. I notice the contrast the elders build: soft words, “gentle,” “tearless” and “without pain,” set against the names of the place below, “all-shrouding” and “Stygian.” The strongest word is “tearless”: it asks for an end without grief or struggle, the opposite of the life of weeping and wandering already shown in the play. Then, effect. In lines 1610–1613, what gentle wish do the elders make, and for whom? My answer: The elders’ prayer is not for victory or for themselves but for the guest they once tried to drive out: the hard place below is named in full, “all-shrouding” and “Stygian,” and against it they set one gentle wish.

segments.activity: A 5-minute teacher model, then 25 minutes of drafting one body paragraph toward the final paper.
segments.script: Writing block (30 minutes). For 5 minutes, model one body paragraph aloud: put “Begone!” (line 216) and lines 1614–1615 on the board and build the exemplar below from them, naming the claim, each quotation and the reasoning as you go. Then students draft for 25 minutes: one body paragraph toward final-paper Prompt 4 (curse and mercy), or toward Prompt 1 (refuge and hospitality), tracing the elders from line 216 to lines 1614–1615. Each paragraph needs a claim, two located quotations (one from the Parodos, one from this ode) and a sentence of reasoning that says what changed. The access supports below stay available.

content.task: Draft one body paragraph toward final-paper Prompt 4 (curse and mercy), or Prompt 1 (refuge and hospitality): how have the elders changed from the Parodos (line 216) to this ode (lines 1614–1615)? Make a claim, quote one line from each ode with its line number, and explain what changed and why it matters.
content.exemplar: In the Parodos the elders answer the name of Oedipus with “Begone!” (line 216) and defend their broken promise with “Heaven’s justice never smites / Him who ill with ill requites” (lines 222–223). In Stasimon 4 the same voices ask the powers below that a man “Wrongfully in life oppressed, / Be he now by Justice blessed” (lines 1614–1615). Justice was first their reason to expel him; now it is the power they call on to bless him. Their mercy is not a denial of his sorrow: they ask the god below to “Speed this stranger to the gloom” (line 1611) gently, and they rest their plea on a new judgment that his suffering was undeserved.

Take two claims to the class and ask which quotation does the most work.

items.text: Why do the elders call Oedipus "wrongfully" oppressed?
items.lookFor: The elders now accept his plea that he acted unknowingly, so the word “Wrongfully” judges his long suffering undeserved rather than earned.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In the Parodos the elders judged Oedipus by his name and tried to expel him. Now they call him “Wrongfully in life oppressed” (line 1614), which means they judge his suffering undeserved. They have accepted the case he argued, that he acted “all unwitting” (line 265), and they ask that he “Be he now by Justice blessed” (line 1615).

items.text: How have the elders changed from “Begone!” in the Parodos to the prayer they sing in this ode? State the inference and one line from this ode.
items.lookFor: The same voices that once drove him out now ask the powers below to let him go gently and to let Justice bless a man they call wrongfully oppressed.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode suggests that the elders’ hospitality has become complete: the men who cried “Begone!” (line 216) now ask the powers below: “By a gentle, tearless doom / Speed this stranger to the gloom” (lines 1610–1611). Their last service to him is this request that his going be without pain, and they add: “Wrongfully in life oppressed, / Be he now by Justice blessed” (lines 1614–1615).

items.text: Find one example of allusion in “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”. What does it reveal about the elders’ prayer for his peace that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: One allusion (Aidoneus, the Goddess dread, the watch-dog of the gates, Tartarus), explained for what it reveals: the elders address each power that could block his way and ask it to let him pass.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders call on the guard dog of the underworld, the “Watch-dog of the gates of hell” (line 1617), and ask that it “let him go / Scathless to the fields below” (lines 1620–1621). The allusion shows that they are thinking through each danger their guest might meet below and pleading with each one. A plain statement that they wish him well would miss how thorough and protective their prayer is.

items.text: How does the tone / mood in “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)” shape what we understand about the elders’ prayer for his peace?
items.lookFor: How the tone, a hushed, reverent prayer, gentle words set against the frightening underworld, shapes our sense that the elders now feel tenderness and protectiveness toward their guest.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The tone is reverent and tender. The elders ask for “a gentle, tearless doom” (line 1610) and that he “enter without pain” (line 1612), while the powers they address are frightening, a monster “Gnarling in thy cavernous lair” (line 1619). The gentleness set against fear shows a protective care for the guest they once wanted to drive away.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “If mortal prayers are…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from the opening lines (1606–1613) with their connotations, such as “dread,” “invisible,” “gentle, tearless” or “all-shrouding,” showing a prayer that faces a frightening place with a gentle wish.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders call the goddess “dread” and “invisible” (line 1607), words that make the powers below frightening and unseen. Against them they set “gentle, tearless” (line 1610). The diction shows a prayer that faces a frightening world honestly and still asks for kindness inside it.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn from asking a gentle way for the stranger to judging his life, “Wrongfully in life oppressed,” and its likely effect: the audience now waits for news of how he fared.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode turns from its request for a gentle way to a judgment of his life: “Wrongfully in life oppressed, / Be he now by Justice blessed” (lines 1614–1615). That turn changes a prayer into a verdict. Because Oedipus has left the stage, its effect is to make the audience wait, with the elders, for word of what happened to him.

items.text: How does “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)” build on “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal link: Oedipus left the stage drawing near “the final gloom / Of Hades,” so the elders, left behind, pray that his way into that gloom be gentle.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The thunder scene ended with Oedipus saying “I am drawing near the final gloom / Of Hades” (lines 1601–1602) as he led the others out. Because he has gone where they cannot follow, the elders do the one thing they can: they ask the powers below to “Speed this stranger to the gloom” (line 1611) gently. His exit causes the prayer.

items.text: In “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the elders’ prayer for his peace, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive inferred from the prayer: the elders ask nothing for themselves, which shows that their concern is now for the guest, and perhaps a wish to make amends for their first hostility.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders ask nothing for themselves; every request is for the stranger, that he “enter without pain” (line 1612) and that the watch-dog “let him go / Scathless” (lines 1620–1621). A fair inference is that they want to make amends: the men who first wanted him gone now use their only power, prayer, on his behalf.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (How have the elders changed since the Parodos?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer to the bell-ringer (how the elders have changed since the Parodos), with a line from each ode.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: My first answer was that the elders have grown used to him. The two odes show something deeper. In the Parodos they cried “Begone!” (line 216); now they call him “Wrongfully in life oppressed” (line 1614). They have changed their judgment of him, not just their feelings. They now believe his suffering was undeserved.

items.text: Where does theme appear in “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”, and how does it connect the elders’ prayer for his peace to the larger concern with refuge and hospitality?
items.lookFor: Where theme appears and how it connects to refuge and hospitality: the elders’ last act of hospitality is to speak for their guest before the gods below.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Hospitality reaches past the stage. The elders cannot follow their guest, so they ask the powers below to receive him well, that he go “Scathless to the fields below” (line 1621). The ode connects the prayer for his peace to hospitality: the hosts who first refused him a seat now ask the gods below to make him welcome.

items.text: Does the change in the Chorus show the play's view of Oedipus? Defend your view.
items.lookFor: A defended view on whether the chorus’s change guides the audience, with lines from early and late, and a counterpoint (the chorus is a character group, not the author).
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: largely yes. The chorus has moved with the audience from fear (“Begone!”, line 216) to sympathy, and its last judgment, that he suffered wrongly in life (lines 1614–1615), echoes what Oedipus argued and what the gods’ summons seems to confirm. Counter-line: the chorus is a group of old men with their own views, and the play also gave his curse on his son its full weight (lines 1426–1427), so the elders’ kindness may not be the whole of the play’s view.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The elders who first drove him away now pray for his peace. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines from the ode, perhaps qualifying “peace”: the elders ask for a painless way and for justice, not only rest.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. They do pray for his peace: “By a gentle, tearless doom / Speed this stranger to the gloom” (lines 1610–1611). But they pray for more than rest; they ask that he be “by Justice blessed” (line 1615), a judgment that his suffering was wrong. Their prayer is for peace and for justice.

items.text: No character acts in “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”; the elders pray. Which of the powers or attitudes the ode presents seems wisest, and which least wise? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to the powers the ode addresses or to the elders’ own conduct, with a line, for example judging by mercy: the elders ask the dread powers below to show the gentleness they once withheld.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of mercy, the elders’ own conduct is the wisest thing in the ode: they ask that the stranger be sped “By a gentle, tearless doom” (line 1610), the mercy they once withheld. The ode presents the guard dog, “Gnarling in thy cavernous lair / At all comers” (lines 1619–1620), as the opposite: a power that treats everyone alike, without mercy. A student could argue that the ode asks this power for an exception, so mercy here has to be won by prayer.

items.text: You are directing “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the elders’ prayer for his peace.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as low, hushed delivery facing the direction Oedipus left, or a sound cue for the watch-dog, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) Sing “By a gentle, tearless doom / Speed this stranger to the gloom” (lines 1610–1611) softly, facing the way Oedipus left, so the prayer follows him off stage. (2) On “Gnarling in thy cavernous lair” (line 1619), have a low drum or growl from below the stage, then silence on “let him go” (line 1620). The audience feels both the danger and the hope that it will be stilled.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1606–1625: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Which creature do the elders ask to let him go? (The watch-dog at the gates, lines 1616–1621.) Why/how: Why do the elders say “If mortal prayers are heard in hell” (line 1606)? (They are unsure whether the gods below listen.) Should/what if: Should the chorus have prayed for Oedipus after he cursed his son? (Answers weigh “Wrongfully in life oppressed,” line 1614, against the curse at lines 1426–1427.)

items.text: Connect “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)”, with its focus on the elders’ prayer for his peace, to guilt and intent: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about guilt and intent, the question’s theme. The link is strong: “Wrongfully in life oppressed” judges that his suffering was undeserved because he did not intend his acts. A strong answer says what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong. The elders now judge that he was “Wrongfully in life oppressed” (line 1614), which accepts the case Oedipus has argued since the Parodos: that he acted without knowledge and is innocent in intent. The judgment is still the elders’ prayer, not the gods’ answer. To strengthen the link, Sophocles would need to show some sign that the powers below accept that judgment.

items.text: Is the allusion in “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)” effective in presenting the elders’ prayer for his peace, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion (do the allusions deepen the prayer or crowd it?), with a line that meets it and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because each allusion names a danger the elders want their guest spared. The guard dog “Who, as legends tell, dost glare” (line 1618) makes the underworld vivid in a few words. Counter-line: modern readers may stumble over Aidoneus, Tartarus and “The son of earth and Tartarus” (line 1623), so the allusions can feel crowded or heavy-handed in a 20-line ode. A strong review decides whether the vivid danger is worth the difficulty.

items.text: Compare how “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)” treats the elders’ prayer for his peace with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (another prayer, hymn or poem for someone who is dying) and one thing the ode sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare a hymn sung at a deathbed for comfort, which usually speaks only of rest and light. The ode sees what such hymns often soften: the place below is frightening, with a guard that snarls “At all comers” (line 1620). The elders do not pretend otherwise; they name the danger and ask that their guest be let through “Scathless” (line 1621). Their comfort is braver because it faces the fear.

items.text: Predict what “Exodos (lines 1626–1831)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, Oedipus leading the way and the elders’ prayer for a gentle end, about what the final scene will bring, without stating an outcome, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: Oedipus left saying he drew “near the final gloom / Of Hades” (lines 1601–1602). Clue 2: the elders pray that he go “By a gentle, tearless doom” (line 1610). A reasonable prediction is that the final scene will bring news of what happened to him, and the class can ask whether the prayer was answered. After reading, students check whether the outcome matches the elders’ hope.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the elders’ prayer for his peace?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a community that once rejected someone now gathers to pray for his peaceful end. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Neighbours who once signed a petition to evict an old man now gather outside the hospital where he lies, praying that his last hours be painless and saying aloud that he was treated unfairly. Two things must stay: the request for a painless end (“Let him enter without pain,” line 1612), and the community’s changed judgment of his life (line 1614).

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

lessonAtAGlance.title: Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)
lessonAtAGlance.objective: Students will analyze how the elders change from the Parodos to this ode by writing a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph that cites at least two quotations—one from the Parodos and one from this ode (Stasimon 4)—and will score at least 80% on the section quiz.
